forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Southwark's treasury team saved £16.5m in 2025-26, though housing account debt costs tripled
news_drafts.lead: Southwark Council's treasury management outperformed its budget by £16.5m in 2025-26, with debt interest coming in £12.7m below forecast and investment income generating £3.8m more than anticipated. The council's £111m average investment portfolio yielded 4.13 per cent, beating the Bank of England's risk-free rate of 4.00 per cent, and peer benchmarking found zero probability of default with returns in the top quartile. However, the housing revenue account, which is funded by rents and kept separate from the council's main budget, saw financing costs reach 44 per cent of its annual revenue—nearly three times the 15 per cent forecast. That 29-point deterioration means the housing account is now spending significantly more of its rental income on debt service than planned, leaving less for maintenance and new building.

findings.headline: The council held £78m more in external investments than forecast, building a stronger cash position than planned.
findings.detail: External investments were £98m at 2025-26 outturn against a forecast of £20m, a surplus of £78m in cash reserves. This excess liquidity likely reflects slippage in capital programme delivery and timing of cash flows. The stronger cash position reduces immediate refinancing exposure.
findings.matters: Higher-than-expected cash reserves reduce immediate liquidity risk, but combined with the capital programme underspend, may signal timing delays in capital delivery or more conservative revenue forecasting than necessary.
findings.figures: External investments 2025-26: £98m actual vs £20m forecast; variance: £78m above forecast

findings.headline: External borrowing precisely matched the Liability Benchmark at year-end 2025-26, indicating optimal debt positioning.
findings.detail: Current loan commitments of £1,208m equalled the calculated Liability Benchmark of £1,208m exactly, with zero variance. This represents optimal treasury positioning under CIPFA's framework: the council is neither over-borrowed (holding surplus cash) nor under-borrowed (exposed to future refinancing risk), and is maximizing the use of internal balance-sheet resources.
findings.matters: Perfect alignment with the Liability Benchmark demonstrates effective treasury management and appropriate calibration of debt to capital needs. Lenders view this as evidence of prudent financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Current loan commitments 2025-26: £1,208m; Liability Benchmark: £1,208m; variance: £0m

findings.headline: The council's borrowing requirement forecast was overstated by £284m or 15% for 2025-26.
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement was forecast at £2,246m for 2025-26 but actual closing CFR was £1,962m. This significant £284m variance reflects either overly conservative planning or capital programme slippage. The undershoot affected planned borrowing drawdown, and the council ended with higher cash reserves than forecast, reducing the need for external borrowing.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need reliable forecasts of borrowing need to assess debt trajectory and credit risk. Significant variance—whether unnecessary debt raised or programme delivery delays—signals forecasting or delivery challenges.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs reached 44% of revenue in 2025-26, nearly three times the 15% forecast.
findings.detail: The HRA's ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream was forecast at 15% but actual outturn was 44%, a deterioration of 29 percentage points. This means the HRA is now spending significantly more of its revenue on debt service than anticipated, materially reducing the revenue available for service delivery and housing investment. The General Fund similarly deteriorated from 8% forecast to 15% actual, though less severely.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the HRA's revenue is being consumed by financing costs at nearly triple the forecast rate, which materially affects HRA financial sustainability and its capacity to deliver services and manage debt repayment.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs: 44% actual 2025-26 vs 15% TMSS estimate; General Fund: 15% actual vs 8% estimate

findings.headline: Investment strategy widened to include building societies and introduce ethical investment screening.
findings.detail: On 12 November 2025, Council Assembly approved changes to add the top 20 building societies by asset size, increase local authority lending limits, and institute ethical screening to exclude investments linked to conflict or military occupation. This expands the counterparty universe and signals a governance framework for non-financial criteria.
findings.matters: Risk management and governance changes indicate how a council operates and what risks it is willing to accept. Widening building society access diversifies counterparty exposure; ethical screening reflects values-driven governance, which some lenders may view as a control signal and others as constraint.
findings.figures: Top 20 building societies by asset size now eligible; ethical investment screening introduced
findings.quote: Council Assembly approved changes to the Investment Strategy on 12 November 2025 to include the top 20 building societies by asset size, to increase the lending limit for local authority investments and to introduce an ethical investment screening process
